paragraphs: At daybreak, a thin frost lay on the reeds along the northern bank of the Fei River. The envoy who had come under a white flag the previous night had spent half the night sitting in the forward tent. His boots had dried by the fire, but his sleeves were still damp. The Qin soldiers had brought him millet porridge; he had eaten only half and left the rest beside his knee. Through the tent flap his attendants heard the drums of morning drill, and each time their faces grew paler.

The envoy’s surname was Tang, and he served as a military secretary in the Beifu Army. Before being admitted to the central command tent, he was taken to a wooden shed. A Qin waterways officer unfolded the chart delivered the night before and pointed out four silted shoals and two channels deep enough for large boats. Tang recognized three of the shoals, but could not be certain about the last channel.

The officer made him write the words “I do not know” on the chart; he did not force him to guess. Then he asked exactly what the Beifu Army intended to move through the passage—troops and horses, baggage carts, or boats carrying the families attached to each camp. If the numbers were wrong by half, the thirty li of open ground might turn out to be a corridor to certain death.

Tang said the fighting boats could make their own way. The greatest concern was the grain vessels and the sick soldiers. He handed over a bamboo tally wound with knotted cord, the knots arranged in convoy order, with a mark Liu Yu had personally cut into the reverse. Two Qin clerks checked it against the military dispatch before leading him into the great tent.

Fu Jian sat by the brazier, with movement registers for both riverbanks spread before him. Fu Rong had been awake all night, and his eyes were bloodshot. Fu Pi stood to the east, one hand resting on his sword hilt. Murong Chui was helped inside, and even after he sat down he kept his fur cloak fastened about his chest. There were no courtly standards in the tent, only wooden counters, maps, and corners of paper soaked through with candle grease.
“You said last night that you would be through within five days,” Fu Jian asked. “What if the wind rises, or the river suddenly floods?”
“General Liu is willing to hold the convoy in designated side channels. If we cannot finish the passage in five days, our army will bear the delay. We will not ask Qin for another li.”
“And if men of the southern army take advantage of our withdrawal to advance north?”

Tang paused. “General Liu will punish those who disobey his orders. If Qin troops see men crossing the boundary, they may issue a warning under the agreement. If the men refuse to withdraw, they may be engaged.”

At this, Fu Pi pushed a black counter marking the ferry into the middle of the channel. “Easy words. The Beifu Army wants to return to Jingkou, while Huan Xuan is in Jiankang. Let this army pass today, and it is Huaibei that will face its threat in years to come.”

The envoy lowered his head and did not argue. Fu Pi turned to his father. “Liu Yu has raised the banner of ‘The South Saves Itself.’ Huan Xuan fears him; the Jin court needs him. Once such a man goes home, he will inevitably gather more and more followers. If we block his way now, perhaps we need not even fight. The great houses of the south may come begging us for terms.”

Fu Jian did not answer at once. Outside, wounded soldiers were being carried past. A stretcher pole struck a tent peg with two muffled knocks. The man had had his foot broken by a sliding stone while dismantling a bridge the day before. A young medical orderly kept warning the bearers to avoid the wheel ruts hardened by frost.
“What will Liu Yu do if we refuse?” Fu Jian asked.

“Find another route east,” Tang replied. “Grain has run out at places all along the Huai. Scouts from north and south will inevitably cross blades. Perhaps Qin gains the advantage; perhaps Beifu does. The civilian boats on both banks will not dare leave harbor, and the villages will be the first to go without salt and rice.”
“How considerate of the common people you have become,” said Fu Pi.

Heat rose in the envoy’s face. “There are men in General Liu’s army who seize grain, too. We can stop some, but not every one of them. That is precisely why we ask Your Majesty to leave us a clear road.”

Murong Chui raised his head and studied the fine branches of water on the chart. The veteran general of the former Yan had commanded men in this country for years. He knew that the palest markings on a marching map often concealed the most impassable ground. He had the waterways chart brought closer and pointed to an unremarkable muddy landing. “If the tide falls here, and seven or eight boats pile up together, with cavalry coming up behind them, how many will die?”
Tang could give no number.

“He has told you how wide a road he wants left open. We ought also to count how many troops it would take to seal that road day and night, and whose fields would have to supply their fodder and water.” Murong Chui set down the bamboo counter and fell into a coughing fit. Fu Rong handed him warm water.

When the old general had drunk, his voice sank still lower. “This road to Jingkou has given Liu Yu his chance to rise. If he truly has ability, sooner or later we will meet him again. Whether killing him now would be easy, I do not know. Whether keeping him trapped by the river is worth the lives of several villages—Your Majesty must decide that for yourself.”

Fu Jian walked to the tent entrance and looked over the rows of camp standards. The wind off the Fei was cold, making the flagpoles creak. Once, when a formation in the Qin army heard that another unit was moving, its first question was often where its own tribal commander had gone. In this year’s camps, each unit first reported its number and then its grain carts; every morning at cockcrow the same route inspectors arrived to examine wheel tracks and wells. As a boy, Fu Jian would never have troubled to remember such small things. Now they had accumulated until they seemed more numerous than all the banners behind him.

He turned and called for Fu Rong. Fu Rong spread out three routes for shifting the camps, calculated the night before. The longest added six li but avoided two fields with occupied homes. Nor were there the two hundred thousand Qin soldiers spoken of in street rumors. Of the eighty thousand serving in this campaign, units were distributed among Shouyang, Huaibei, and the roads of approach. Less than half were stationed by the river; the rest needed only to adjust their screening positions. The orders for breaking camp could be in the hands of the unit commanders three days in advance.
“Choose the longer way around,” Fu Jian said.
Fu Pi could contain himself no longer. “Imperial Father!”

“You fear that Liu Yu will become a formidable enemy.” Fu Jian looked at him. “So do I. But what he asks now is to bring his men away from the river. If I give my word and then strike him from behind while he is crossing, who will ever trust the Compact for Crossing the River, even if we write another hundred clauses into it?”

Fu Pi was silent. His father went on. “You will remain with central command and check the reports from every camp. If any unit leaves its assigned route without orders, you will deal with it. You have commanded an advance before. This time, learn how to manage a withdrawal.”

The envoy was led to the outer gallery to await the documents. Qin clerks copied out, point by point, the boundaries on each bank, the starting and ending times for the withdrawal, the convoy route, and the five-day limit, preparing two copies. Qin did not recognize this as a treaty of peace, and Liu Yu had no authority to make a state compact on behalf of the Jin court. Yet for this stretch of bank and this one movement of troops, which banner must retreat beyond which boundary stake was written down with greater precision than many treaties between states. The Qin side affixed the camp seal; Tang signed for the southern army and took his copy back across. A small boat crossed the middle of the river three times to deliver the Jin endorsement.

On the first day the medical carts set out. Porters carrying sick men were given a bowl of warm gruel before collecting folded, numbered cloth passes. One asked in a whisper whether the Jin army had already fought its way across. An old one-eyed soldier thrust the cloth into his hand and told him to look south: the cavalry screens were still there, the crossbow lines were still there. Where were these pursuers supposed to be?

A soldier’s wife followed the medical carts. She pushed her son’s thin cotton coat into the bottom of a wagon, afraid the troops would think the presence of a family unbecoming to soldiers. The officer checking the wagon pulled out the coat and asked only how old the boy was and whether he could endure the cold road. Then he added a wooden token entitling the child to hot water. The woman stared, unable to take it, until an orderly urged her to depart. Only then did she close her hand around the token. Someone by the marching road saw this and quietly passed up the wheat cakes left over from the day before.

The second day belonged to the baggage train. Hundreds of ox carts stood in camp-number order along the frost-white road. Their axles had already been oiled, but from time to time still emitted a shrill scrape. A convoy belonging to an old imperial-clan unit set out early. Its captain laid his riding crop across a road guard’s shoulder and demanded to know how some petty clerk with a register dared obstruct a banner inherited from his ancestors.

The guard was a man from Hedong, missing two fingers on his right hand. He neither stepped aside nor cursed in return. Instead he raised his wooden pass and asked the captain to read the appointed time. The captain shoved him away. The baggage wagons crowded into the bridge approach and nearly pushed a cart carrying wounded soldiers from the preceding column into the ditch.

Fu Pi happened to be inspecting an adjoining road. After taking one look at the order of carts, he summoned the captain to his horse. “If you want precedence, go back to Chang’an and argue for it at the army office. If the wagon in front overturns today, you will be the first to pay for it with your life.” He ordered an officer to record the violation and had the convoy backed off the bridge. Ten years earlier, the imperial-clan captain might not have obeyed anyone except Fu Pi. Today, even Fu Pi showed him no favoritism.

From a watchtower on the southern bank, a Beifu commander pointed to the dust streaming north and asked permission for a night attack. Liu Yu handed him the viewing tube and told him to look at the cavalry still holding the southern edge of the old camp. The scouts reported that those men continued their nightly roll calls, and the sound of hooves outside the camp had never ceased.

Liu Yu ordered his river forces to do nothing but clear the passage for the boats. Not one man was to cross a boundary stake. When the soldiers failed to understand, he had the grain officer read aloud the pay owed to the southern army over the past three months. Those sums would not grow smaller if they captured an empty stockade while the enemy withdrew. And if battle did break out, Jingkou could not support the families of even half his men.

On the afternoon of the third day, the Qin army came close to disorder. Behind the camp men were dismantling a watchtower when a wet timber slipped from its frame and struck a warhorse, sending it rearing and screaming. Fu Rong’s mount shied as well, and the central command’s great banner tilted half a foot. The rear ranks could not see the wooden structure; they saw only the leaning banner and heard someone cry, “The Duke of Yangping has fallen!” Within moments this had become “The Jin army is in the rear camp!” A squad of Xianbei archers drew their bowstrings, and a Di soldier seized a bow arm. The two shouted at each other, faces crimson, but at that very moment both heard the camp’s assembly drum.
Three long beats, two short. Form up and await orders.

The soldier assigned to relay the drum signal was so young that he nearly struck the wrong rhythm the first time. An old drummer beside him caught his hand and guided him until the beat was steady. By unit number, the columns gathered where they stood. Teamsters pulled their oxen toward the ditch; crossbowmen guarded the southern opening. Only one small detachment took the wrong road and blundered against the fence of the new camp before patrolling horsemen led them back. Fu Rong leaped from his horse and righted the leaning flagstaff himself. When all the reports were in, he crossed the churned mud left by the wheels and picked up a broken wooden wedge.

“Keep this on my desk today,” he told an accompanying military clerk. “Write down which watchtower it came from, who hurried the dismantling, and who failed to check the fastenings. If we question only the man who shouted the wrong thing, the army will be thrown into confusion again tomorrow.”

The men gradually settled. When they saw the soldier who first cried out being led away, some thought he would surely be beheaded. But that night’s military register classified his offense as a panicked false report: he was sentenced to guard the storehouse and lose a month’s reward allowance. The works officer who had failed to inspect the tower was separately held to serious account. By the time Fu Rong reported to Fu Jian, the wedge was in a little gray cloth pouch. Fu Jian felt the fragment of wood and ordered it deposited at the army office. He did not wish to forget that however long an army had drilled, half a piece of rotten timber could still alarm thousands of men.

On the fourth day, the central command shifted camp. The fires by the river were lit at their usual hour, though the cooking hearths were steadily growing empty. Liu Yu sent men into the abandoned stockades to inspect the wells. They found wooden water-testing markers and signs delimiting where water could be drawn. Several porters said the Qin soldiers had even straightened the vegetable beds they had trampled before leaving.

That did not mean they had never mistreated anyone. A villager came to complain that a borrowed donkey had not been returned. A military officer stationed there by the Qin Secretariat followed the receipt to the new camp, brought the donkey back at dusk, and paid half a sack of feed in compensation. The village woman stroked the animal’s ear and found a patch of frostbite upon it. She set the feed beside the donkey without a word of thanks.

By twilight on the fifth day, the remaining cavalry withdrew from the riverbank, section by section. Fu Pi still feared the army opposite would seize territory and asked to leave a troop of roving horsemen secretly following the Jin boats. Fu Jian refused. He told his son to look at the last boundary stone on the north bank. A black horizontal line had been painted across it: Qin troops stop here. Thirty li farther north stood the new camps, with their supply roads intact. On the water to the south, Beifu boatmen were testing the night tide.
“What if they break their word?” Fu Pi asked.
“Then tomorrow’s military dispatch will tell us,” Fu Jian said. “Today we do what we agreed to do today.”

He walked to the edge of the high platform and rested his palm on its weather-dried railing. Twenty years ago everyone here would have waited for him to decide whether to advance or retreat. Now every unit in the withdrawal had its own designation and travel papers. Fu Jian remembered Wang Meng, sick in bed, entrusting him with a promise of ten years. He remembered, too, Fu Hong later proposing a system of review and rejection of imperial orders in Chang’an. An emperor could still move tens of thousands of men with one edict; he could no longer listen to every drumbeat for every soldier, steady every cart of wounded, or stop every panicked horse. That those men had done their own appointed work today was what gave him the courage to bring his standards back.

The last horsemen rode away, leaving warmth in the ashes of the old Qin hearths. From the southern bank Liu Yu watched the long rows of camp lights kindle again along the northern ridges. He did not at once order his vanguard boats to sail. Only when the boundary inspectors from both sides had reported that flags and stakes matched did he let the sick soldiers and grain vessels go first. During the night passage across the Fei, the Beifu men could hear the distant metal gongs of Qin sentries changing watch. None of them spoke of a defeated army.

Before dawn every southern vessel had passed. As the last boatmen prepared to pull apart the temporary planks at the landing, they saw a family returning from the hills and standing on the muddy bank. An elderly couple led a little grandson; several empty baskets hung from their shoulders. They were staring at the brushwood hut that had once been theirs. The door was gone, but the roof beams remained. Stones covered the well in front, and on the top stone someone had written, “Safe to drink.” The child could not recognize all the characters and asked his grandfather to read them. The old man read them aloud, then scooped up and drank a dipper of cold water.

He wanted to ask someone whether this year’s land tax should go to Qin officials or Jin officials. The armies on both banks had already gone far away, and there was no one to answer. Water spilled over the rim of his dipper, ran across his frost-cracked fingers, and returned to the earth. He replaced the cover over the well and called his family to help mend the roof.
The Fei still divided two courts. Yet by keeping their word for those five days, the two armies had spared the people along its banks at least one morning.
